Outer connective tissue.description: The adventitia is the outer layer of the thoracic oesophagus. It is loose connective tissue that blends into the surrounding chest and carries the blood vessels, lymphatics and nerves that supply the wall. This part has no serosa, unlike the stomach and intestine.
clinical: The thoracic oesophagus has no serosa, so a cancer growing outward can invade directly into the trachea, aorta and other chest structures.

Squamous epithelium.description: This is the lining of the oesophagus: a thick stack of cell layers, flattened only at the surface, resting on a basement membrane. Cells made by the basal layer move upward to replace the surface cells as they wear away. The lining is not keratinised, so its surface cells keep their nuclei, unlike skin.
clinical: Most oesophageal cancers worldwide are squamous cell carcinomas, which arise from this lining. Smoking and heavy alcohol use are major risk factors.
Long-term acid reflux can replace the lower oesophageal lining with intestinal-type columnar cells (Barrett oesophagus). This raises the risk of adenocarcinoma.

Muscularis externa.description: The muscularis externa is the muscle wall of this part of the oesophagus. In this lower section it is smooth muscle, arranged as an inner circular layer and an outer longitudinal layer. Waves of contraction through both layers (peristalsis) push food toward the stomach.
clinical: In achalasia the lower oesophageal muscle fails to relax when swallowing, so food collects in the oesophagus and the normal wave-like contraction is lost.

Oesophageal glands.description: The oesophagus has compound mucous glands in the submucosa. Their blind-ending secretory branches drain into a collecting duct, and each duct passes through the muscularis mucosae and mucosa to open on the surface, releasing mucus that lubricates food.

Mucosa.description: The lamina propria is the loose connective tissue under the lining, forming low papillae that rise into the epithelium. The muscularis mucosae is a thin layer of smooth muscle lying below it, and the gland ducts pass through it on the way to the surface.
clinical: Forceful or repeated vomiting can tear the mucosa near the junction with the stomach, which may cause bleeding.

Vessels.description: The wall has its own blood supply. The submucosal artery and vein run through the submucosa, capillary loops in the lamina propria nourish the lining, and lymphatic vessels carry fluid away from the wall.
clinical: Dilated veins in the lower oesophageal submucosa form when portal hypertension, for example from cirrhosis, forces blood into collateral veins that link the portal and systemic circulations. These veins can rupture and bleed heavily.

Enteric plexuses.description: The enteric plexuses are networks of nerve cells and fibres inside the wall that control movement and secretion largely independently of the brain. The myenteric plexus lies between the two muscle layers and drives peristalsis. The submucosal plexus, which is sparse in this part of the tube, lies in the submucosa and mainly controls secretion.
clinical: Achalasia is linked to loss of inhibitory nerve cells in the myenteric plexus, so the lower oesophageal muscle does not relax properly during swallowing.

Submucosa.description: The submucosa is the connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa. Its core supports the longitudinal folds of the lining and carries the glands, blood vessels and nerves of the wall.
clinical: Early oesophageal cancer is staged partly by how deep it grows. Reaching the submucosa marks a more advanced stage than staying in the mucosa.

parts.description: Basal epithelial nuclear profiles are the nuclei of the basal cells, the deepest row of cells in the oesophageal lining, which sit directly on the basement membrane. Basal cell nuclei are round to oval and look darker than the nuclei of the cells above them. In a section, look for this dark, tightly packed row of nuclei at the base of the squamous epithelium.

The basal squamous epithelial layer, or stratum basale, is the single row of cells at the bottom of the oesophageal lining, resting on the basement membrane. These cells divide continually and include the stem cells, so new cells are pushed upward to replace the surface cells as they are shed. Because this row is where new cells are made, dividing cells, seen as mitotic figures (dark clumps of chromosomes), are most often found here in a section.

The basement membrane is the thin sheet of extracellular matrix that separates the epithelium from the lamina propria (loose connective tissue) beneath it. It is made of collagen type IV and laminin, which anchor the basal cells and act as a selective filter. In a light-microscope section it is a thin, pale-pink line at the base of the lining, most clearly seen with the periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, which turns it magenta.

The circular fascicles are the bundles of muscle fibres in the inner layer of the muscularis externa, the thick muscle coat of the oesophagus. They run round the tube at right angles to its length, so their contraction narrows the lumen, the central channel of the tube, and drives food onward. In the lower third of the oesophagus they are smooth muscle, and in a transverse section their nuclei look long and lie in parallel rows.

Flattened superficial nuclear profiles are the nuclei of the surface cells of the oesophageal lining, the cells that face the lumen (the central channel). These cells are flat, and their nuclei are squeezed into thin shapes lying parallel to the surface. In a section, look for a thin row of flattened nuclei along the top edge of the lining, the most superficial part of the squamous epithelium.

The inner circular smooth muscle is the inner of the two muscle layers of the muscularis externa, the muscle coat of the oesophagus. Lying just outside the submucosa, its fibres run round the tube, so their contraction narrows the lumen and squeezes food onward. In the lower third of the oesophagus these fibres are smooth muscle, so their movement is involuntary.

keys: Inner circular smooth muscle dissection cover
parts.description: The inner circular muscle is a continuous sleeve of muscle, smooth in the lower oesophagus, that encircles the lumen between the submucosa and the myenteric plexus (a nerve network). Its contraction narrows the tube behind a food bolus, pushing the food downward during peristalsis. In a longitudinal section its fibres appear as round cross-sections, whereas the outer longitudinal layer appears as long, elongated fibres.

Intermediate epithelial nuclear profiles are the nuclei of the intermediate cells, the many-sided (polyhedral) cells lying between the basal layer and the surface. These cells are joined to their neighbours by many desmosomes (small anchoring junctions), which give them a spiny outline under the light microscope. Their nuclei are round to oval and sit near the middle of each cell, forming several rows in the thick middle of the lining.

The intermediate squamous epithelial layers, also called the stratum spinosum or prickle-cell layer, make up the thick middle of the oesophageal lining. They lie above the basal layer, and as their cells are pushed upward they change from cuboidal to larger, flatter shapes. In a section they form a broad band of several cell rows between the dark basal row and the flattened surface cells.

Local lymphatic vessels are the thin-walled channels that drain tissue fluid, called lymph, from the lining and wall of the oesophagus. The smallest of them, the lymphatic capillaries, lie in the lamina propria and submucosa, and their walls are so thin that fluid can seep in easily. In a section, look for a wide, pale lumen with a very thin wall and no red blood cells.

The longitudinal fascicles are the bundles of muscle fibres in the outer layer of the muscularis externa, running parallel to the length of the oesophagus. Their contraction shortens the tube and, working with the circular layer, helps move food towards the stomach. In a transverse section they are cut across, so they look like small, rounded profiles on the outside of the muscle coat.

The muscularis mucosae is a thin layer of smooth muscle in the deepest part of the mucosa, lying between the lamina propria above and the submucosa below. Its contraction helps throw the lining into the longitudinal folds seen when the empty oesophagus is opened. Gland ducts from the submucosa pass through it on their way to the surface, so look for ducts cutting through this thin muscle band.

The myenteric connective tissue plane is the thin layer of loose connective tissue that separates the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa. It carries the blood vessels and nerve fibres of the myenteric plexus between the two muscle coats, so the coats can move relative to each other. In a section, look for a pale, sparsely cellular line between the two smooth muscle layers.

keys: Myenteric connective tissue plane dissection cover
parts.description: The myenteric connective tissue plane is a thin sheet of loose connective tissue between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle coats of the oesophagus. It is the natural plane along which these two layers can be separated in dissection, and it houses the myenteric plexus of nerve cells. In a section it shows as a pale, lightly stained line separating two pink bands of smooth muscle.

The myenteric plexus, also called Auerbach's plexus, is a network of nerve cells and fibres lying between the inner circular and outer longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa. It controls the rhythm and strength of the muscle contractions that drive peristalsis, largely without input from the brain. Under the microscope, look for small clusters of nerve cell bodies, called ganglia, in the connective tissue between the two muscle layers.

The outer longitudinal smooth muscle is the outer of the two muscle layers of the muscularis externa in the lower oesophagus, lying just beneath the adventitia. Its fibres run parallel to the length of the tube, so their contraction shortens the oesophagus and helps push food along it. Working with the inner circular layer, it forms the wave of peristalsis that carries the food bolus down to the stomach.

keys: Papillary capillary loops and basal channels
parts.description: Papillary capillary loops are the tiny blood vessels that rise into the lamina propria papillae, the finger-like projections pushing up beneath the lining. The basal channels at the base of the papillae form part of the same local network. Because the squamous epithelium has no blood vessels of its own, these capillaries supply the basal cells with oxygen and nutrients. In a section, look for red blood cells packed in narrow, looped channels at the tips of the papillae.

Patent (open) gland ducts are the narrow tubes that carry mucus from the submucosal glands up through the muscularis mucosae and lamina propria to open on the surface of the lining. Their wall is made of small cuboidal cells, which distinguishes them from the mucus-secreting cells of the glands. In a section, look for a small round lumen with a cuboidal wall passing through the thin muscle layer.

The submucosal plexus, also called Meissner's plexus, is a network of nerve cells and fibres in the submucosa, the connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa. It mainly controls secretion and local blood flow, rather than the movement that the myenteric plexus drives. In the oesophagus this plexus is poorly developed, so its ganglia are few and small, and it is much less conspicuous than the myenteric plexus.

The submucosal artery is a medium-sized artery that runs through the submucosa, the connective tissue layer beneath the mucosa. Its branches climb up to form the capillary network that supplies the mucosa, and it also feeds the glands and nerves in this layer. In a section, its thick, muscular wall and round, open lumen separate it from the thinner-walled vein that often lies beside it.

The submucosal vein is a thin-walled vessel in the submucosa, usually running alongside the artery. It drains blood from the mucosa and submucosa into the larger veins outside the oesophagus. In a section, look for a wide, thin-walled lumen that often looks collapsed or irregular, unlike the round, muscular artery beside it.

The superficial nucleated squamous layers are the upper cells of the oesophageal lining, forming the top of the stratified squamous epithelium that faces the lumen. Unlike the keratinised skin, these cells keep their nuclei, which is why the layers are described as nucleated. The cells are flattened and are shed into the lumen as they wear away, being replaced from below.
